title: Vector helpers
text:
Vector helpers are evaluated once per group on whole columns. Use them as mutate(), filter(), and summarise() arguments. They follow R’s NA rules: a summary returns NA when its input has an NA unless na_rm: true, ranks keep NA, and cumulative functions stay NA after the first NA.
The first argument is the input column. A string there is a column name. It can also be col('x'), another helper, or a row closure. Later arguments are values. ->map(fn ($value, $r) => ...) transforms a helper’s result row by row.

title: Vector helpers
text:
Summaries



Helper
Value




n()
Rows in the group


n_distinct('x', 'y')
Distinct values or combinations


sum, mean, median
As in R


sd, variance
Sample statistics (n − 1)


quantile('x', 0.9), iqr('x')
Type 7 quantiles, R’s default


min, max
Smallest and largest values


first, last, nth('x', 2)
Values by position, with default:


any, all
Logical summaries with NA logic



With the phit extension loaded, mean, sd, variance, median, and quantile use it. Without it they run in PHP and give the same results.

title: Vector helpers
text:
Window functions







Helper
Value




lag('x', n:, default:, order_by:), lead(...)
Shifted values


row_number(), row_number('x')
Row numbers, or ranks with ties broken by position


min_rank, dense_rank
Ranks; wrap the column in desc() to reverse


percent_rank, cume_dist
Ranks scaled to [0, 1]


ntile('x', 4)
Buckets of near-equal size


cumsum, cumprod, cummin, cummax, cummean
Running values


cumall, cumany
Running logical values


consecutive_id('x')
A new id each time the value changes


order_by('t', cumsum('x'))
A window function evaluated in another order




Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv'))
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->school === 'school-01')
    ->arrange('study_hours')
    ->mutate(
        prev: lag('score'),
        change: lag('score')->map(fn ($prev, $r) => $prev === null ? null : round($r->score - $prev, 2)),
        running_mean: cummean('score'),
        rank: min_rank(desc('score')),
        pct: percent_rank('score'),
        quartile: ntile('score', 4),
    )
    ->select('study_hours', 'score', 'prev', 'change', 'running_mean', 'rank', 'pct', 'quartile')
    ->head(8);


echo DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv')
    |> filter(fn ($r) => $r->school === 'school-01')
    |> arrange('study_hours')
    |> mutate(
        prev: lag('score'),
        change: lag('score')->map(fn ($prev, $r) => $prev === null ? null : round($r->score - $prev, 2)),
        running_mean: cummean('score'),
        rank: min_rank(desc('score')),
        pct: percent_rank('score'),
        quartile: ntile('score', 4),
    )
    |> select('study_hours', 'score', 'prev', 'change', 'running_mean', 'rank', 'pct', 'quartile')

Conditionals and NA







Helper
Use




if_else(cond, yes, no, missing:)
Vectorized if/else


case_when([cond, value], ..., default:)
The first true condition wins


replace_when('x', [cond, value], ...)

recode_values('x', [from, to], ..., default:)
Map values; also from: / to: lookup lists


replace_values('x', [from, to], ...)

dplyr’s superseded recoder, matching values by name

The first non-NA value

Inclusive range test


near('x', y)
Equality within floating-point tolerance




Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],
]))
    ->mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),
        visits: coalesce('visits', 0),
        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),
        capped: replace_when('visits', [fn ($r) => $r->visits > 10, 10]),
        any_flag: when_any(fn ($r) => $r->state === 'CA', fn ($r) => $r->visits === 0),
    );


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],

    |> mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),

        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),

Strings and dates
text: phplyr re-exports phibble’s stringr and lubridate functions. They build expressions, so they work in memory and, where a SQL translation exists, on database tables. Their results are checked against stringr 1.6.0 and lubridate 1.9.5.

title: Strings and dates
text:
Strings
As in stringr, a pattern is a regular expression. fixed('a.b') matches the text literally, and regex('ab', ignore_case: true) sets options.







Function
Value




str_detect(x, p, negate:), str_starts, str_ends
Whether the pattern matches


str_count(x, p)
Number of matches


str_extract(x, p)
The first match, or NA


str_extract_all(x, p), str_split(x, p)
A list per row (a list-column)


str_split_i(x, p, i)
The i-th piece; negative counts from the end


str_replace(x, p, r), str_replace_all
Replace the first or every match; \1 refers to a group


str_pad(x, width, side:, pad:)
Pad to a width


str_trunc(x, width, side:, ellipsis:)
Truncate with an ellipsis


str_to_title, str_to_upper, str_to_lower
Change case


str_squish, str_trim(x, side)
Remove whitespace


str_length, str_sub(x, start, end)
Length and substrings



str_replace, str_pad, and str_split shadow PHP built-ins in files that import them.

text:
Dates and times







Function
Value




ymd, dmy, mdy, ymd_hms, dmy_hms, mdy_hms (tz:)
Parse text; failures give NA


parse_date_time(x, ['Ymd HMS', 'dmY HMS'])
Parse with lubridate orders


year, month, day, yday, quarter, hour, minute, second
Parts


wday(x, week_start:)
Day of the week; Sunday is 1 unless week_start: 1


floor_date(x, unit), ceiling_date, round_date
Round to 'hour', '15 minutes', 'week', 'month', and so on


seconds(n) … years(n)
Periods: col('d')->add(months(1))


difftime(x, y, units:)
The difference as a number


with_tz(x, tz), force_tz(x, tz)
Change the displayed zone, or the zone itself


today(tz:), now(tz:)
The current date or time



Month and year arithmetic that lands on a date that doesn’t exist, such as January 31 plus one month, gives NA, as in lubridate. Subtracting dates gives days, and subtracting datetimes gives seconds. Date columns stay dates through these functions. Phibble\Expr\Clock::freeze() fixes today() and now() in tests.

title: Models
Databases and expressions
text:
phplyr’s helpers build inspectable expressions whenever their arguments are column names, literals, or other helpers. col('x') refers to a column, and methods combine expressions with operators:
filter(col('price')->mul(1.1)->gt(100), col('brand')->isIn(['a', 'b']))
mutate(margin: col('price')->sub(col('cost'))->div(col('price')))
mutate(dev: col('score')->sub(mean('score')))      // mean() recycles per group
The operator methods are add, sub, mul, div, mod, pow, neg, eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge, and, or, not, isNa, isIn, between, and desc. Scalar helpers include round, abs, sqrt, exp, log, log10, floor, ceiling, is_na, as_int, as_float, as_string, as_bool, paste, and paste0. Several of these names shadow PHP built-ins in files that import them. The string and date helpers are expressions too.
An expression is a Phibble\Expr tree. Verbs pass it to the table. The in-memory DataFrame evaluates it with dplyr’s semantics, and a database table compiles it to SQL. A helper given a PHP closure still works, but it is evaluated in PHP.
mutate(_keep: 'used') and _keep: 'unused' need expression arguments, because phplyr reads the columns an expression uses from the tree.

title: Databases and expressions
Performance
text: phplyr is a thin layer. Each verb calls one or two methods of the table it is given, so the backend determines how fast a pipeline runs. This page reports timings for phibble’s shared benchmark workloads on DataFrame and SQLite, and for three phplyr pipelines on DataFrame, PolarsTable, and SQLite, and gives guidance on choosing a backend.

title: Performance
text:
Method
bench/harness.php runs each workload twice: as a phplyr pipeline, and as the same calls made directly on the table. bench/generate.php writes the data. It is the same generator and seed as phibble’s bin/bench, so the two harnesses time identical data:

events.csv: 1,000,000 rows of id, key (10,000 distinct values), g (8 labels), x (float, about 2% NA), and t (datetime).
dims.csv: 100,000 rows of key, label, and w.

php bench/generate.php 1000000
php bench/harness.php --backend=frame --runs=3
php bench/harness.php --backend=sqlite --runs=3
Each timing includes collect(), so lazy backends do their work inside the timer. The numbers below are medians of three runs on an Apple Silicon Mac with PHP 8.5 and phibble fa978f6.

title: Performance
text:
phplyr’s overhead
At 100,000 rows, the phplyr pipeline and the direct calls differed by at most 5% on every workload and backend, which is within run-to-run noise. Grouped slices, pivot_*(), and complete() build on the same table methods and carry the same small overhead.

title: Performance
text:
Choosing a backend

In-memory DataFrame suits data that fits in memory, up to a few million rows. Expression arguments are the fastest form: a grouped summary with mean('x') runs about four times faster than the same summary written as closures, because phibble computes it in one pass without building a table per group.
A database table (Phibble\tbl()) avoids loading the data into PHP. With expressions, filter() and summarise() run in the database, and only the result reaches PHP, so memory stays small. This is the right choice when the data lives in a database or doesn’t fit in memory. For data already in memory, a frame is faster: these timings exclude loading, and reading the 1M-row CSV into a frame takes about 1.4 seconds. Pipelines that return every row (mutate(), arrange(), unfiltered joins) spend most of their database time transferring rows to PHP.
Closures on a database table load all rows first and then run in memory. Use col() expressions and phplyr’s helpers to keep the work in SQL.
SQLite columns need declared types. PDO binds values as strings. In an untyped column, SQLite stores them as text and compares numbers as text.
PolarsTable (phibble’s Polars backend, on the phpolars extension) runs the verbs in Polars, 10 to 100 times faster than DataFrame, and pays mainly for bringing rows back into PHP. See below.

title: Performance
text:
PolarsTable
bench/backends.php times three phplyr pipelines on DataFrame, PolarsTable, and SQLite, and checks that all three backends return the same rows. It is adapted from phpolars’ benchmark script. The pipelines are:

A: filter, join a store lookup, two-key summarise, then a ranking window.
B: grouped lag(order_by:), cumsum(), and a share of the group total over all rows.
C: pipeline A with a closure in filter().

Times are the best of three runs through collect(), on an Apple M5 Ultra with Homebrew PHP 8.5, phibble 9655e2a, and Polars 0.55.2 at two threads. In every case the three backends returned the same rows. The full results, with all repeat timings and version details, are in benchmarks/backends-results.json.



Pipeline, 1M rows
DataFrame (s)
PolarsTable (s)
SQLite (s)




A: reduce to a ranked summary
0.62
0.06
0.47


B: windows over every row
1.32
0.43
3.52


C: A with a closure
1.09
0.89
1.97



The verbs themselves are fast in Polars. Most of PolarsTable’s time goes to converting results back to PHP values: about 0.2 seconds per million rows of plain columns, plus about 0.5 seconds per million values of a datetime column, because each value becomes a PHP DateTimeImmutable. A pipeline that returns every row of a table with a datetime column can therefore be slower on PolarsTable than on DataFrame. In phibble’s harness, mutate() and left_join() returning 1M rows took 1.3 seconds on PolarsTable against 0.3 seconds on DataFrame.
A closure makes PolarsTable convert the data to a DataFrame and back, which costs about a second per million rows. Pipeline C runs its closure step that way.
Use PolarsTable when a pipeline reduces the data before collecting (summaries, filters, distinct(), or a join followed by a summary), when it chains several steps, or when the data starts in Polars: PolarsTable::fromPolars(Phpolars\read_csv($path)) skips phibble’s CSV parse. Keep the pipeline in expressions so every step stays in Polars.

title: Getting started
Getting started
Getting started
Getting started
text:
Chaining verbs
A verb such as filter(...) returns a closure that takes a table. phplyr runs a sequence of verbs in three ways, and all three give the same result.

Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


phplyr($t) starts a chain. Each method runs the phplyr verb of that name with the same arguments, and get() returns the table:
$out = phplyr($schools)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)
    ->arrange(desc('score'))
    ->get();
echo prints a chain’s table directly. A verb whose result isn’t a table, such as pull(), n_groups(), or lm(), returns that result and ends the chain. ->pipe($closure) applies a closure of your own and continues.


The pipe operator calls each closure with the value on its left:
$out = $schools
    |> filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)
    |> arrange(desc('score'));



pipe() applies the closures in order and works on every PHP version:
$out = pipe($schools, filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80), arrange(desc('score')));
// is the same as
$out = arrange(desc('score'))(filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)($schools));
The rest of this guide shows each example both as a method chain and with |>. The two are interchangeable.
Columns are named with strings: write 'score' where dplyr takes a bare score.

title: Getting started
Getting started
text:
Named arguments and options
Verbs that create columns name them with PHP named arguments: mutate(total: ...), summarise(n: n()). dplyr’s dot-prefixed options are written with a leading underscore, because PHP named arguments cannot start with a dot: _by, _keep, _before, _after, _groups, _keep_all, and _by_group.
PHP does not allow positional arguments after named ones. Put across() and other positional arguments first: summarise(across(...), n: n()).

title: Getting started
text:
Printing and inspecting
echo prints a frame. glimpse() prints one line per column and passes the table through, so it can sit inside a pipeline. pull('x') returns a column as a PHP list, and $frame->toRows() returns all rows as arrays.

title: Development
text:
The tests use Pest and run under PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. They call verbs through pipe(), so they parse on every version. tests/Pipe/ holds the tests written with |>; bin/test leaves them out before PHP 8.5.
composer install
bin/test                 # loads .ext/libphit.dylib when present
NO_EXT=1 bin/test        # pure-PHP descriptive statistics
PHP=/path/to/php83 bin/test
The method chain’s @method list in src/Chain.php is generated. After adding or changing a verb, run bin/chain-docblock; a test fails while the list is out of date.
Most tests compare phplyr with R. The scripts in tests/r/ run the same pipelines with dplyr and tidyr and write JSON fixtures to tests/Fixtures/:
Rscript tests/r/reference.R   # single-table verbs, windows, across, tidyselect
Rscript tests/r/joins.R       # joins and rowwise
Rscript tests/r/tidyr.R       # tidyr verbs
Rscript tests/r/rows.R        # set operations, rows_*(), dplyr 1.2 helpers
Rscript tests/r/models.R      # lm() and glm() coefficients

title: Development
text:
Documentation
The site is a Quarto project in docs/. Code examples live in docs/examples/*.php. bin/docs-examples runs each one with docs/data as the working directory and writes docs/examples/_<name>.md with the code and its output, which the pages include. Rendering never executes PHP.
An example uses |>, and docs/examples/<name>.chain.php beside it is the same example as a method chain. bin/docs-examples runs both and fails if their output differs. The page shows the two in tabs, with the output once.
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/docs-examples   # refresh example output
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/render-docs     # examples, quarto render, publish to docs/
GitHub Pages serves the rendered site from main:/docs.

title: Coming from dplyr

Syntax translation
In R, verbs are chained with %>% or |>. In PHP, they are chained as methods, phplyr($t)->filter(...)->arrange(...), or on PHP 8.5 with |>. The table below shows single calls.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
Conventions

Dot-arguments. dplyr’s .by, .keep, .before, .after, .groups, .keep_all, .by_group, .direction, .id, and .remove are written _by, _keep, and so on. A column whose name starts with an underscore cannot be created through a named argument.
Positions are 1-based, as in R: pull(1) is the first column, pull(-1) the last, and slice(1, 3) the first and third rows of each group.
var() is variance(), because var is a reserved word in PHP.
count, min, and max shadow PHP’s built-ins in files that import them.
Group order follows dplyr: groups are sorted by key, factors by level order, and NA last. _by also sorts groups (dplyr keeps first-appearance order for .by).

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
across() functions
R passes a vector to every across() function. PHP closures have no such convention, so phplyr decides what a function receives:

A phplyr helper passed as a first-class callable, such as mean(...) or lag(...), is called with each column’s name.
In summarise(), any other closure receives the column’s values as a list.
In mutate(), a closure receives one value at a time. If its first parameter is typed array, it receives the whole column instead.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
Not supported

Bare column names and tidy evaluation. Columns are strings, and expressions are closures or phplyr helpers.
mutate(.keep = "used") and .keep = "unused" with closures. These work with expression arguments such as col('x')->mul(2), whose columns can be read. A PHP closure does not expose the columns it reads.
cur_group(), cur_column(), and cur_data(). cur_group_id() and cur_group_rows() are supported in mutate(), summarise(), and reframe().
Data frame columns, across(.unpack), and nest_join().
Superseded functions such as top_n(), sample_n(), the scoped _at, _if, and _all variants, and recode(). Use slice_max(), slice_sample(), across(), and recode_values().

text:
Clinic calls by staffing
The clinic data has visitors, staff, and calls for 120 days. The example bands staffing and visitor volume, averages calls, and widens the result into a cross-tabulation.

Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


// Calls by staffing level and visitor volume, as a cross-tabulation.
echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv('clinic.csv'))
    ->mutate(
        staffing: case_when([fn ($r) => $r->staff < 4, 'low'], [fn ($r) => $r->staff < 6, 'mid'], default: 'high'),
        volume: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visitors >= 250, 'busy', 'quiet'),
    )
    ->group_by('staffing', 'volume')
    ->summarise(mean_calls: mean('calls'), _groups: 'drop')
    ->mutate(mean_calls: fn ($r) => round($r->mean_calls, 2))
    ->pivot_wider(names_from: 'volume', values_from: 'mean_calls', names_sort: true)
    ->arrange(fn ($r) => array_search($r->staffing, ['low', 'mid', 'high']));


// Calls by staffing level and visitor volume, as a cross-tabulation.
echo DataFrame::fromCsv('clinic.csv')
    |> mutate(
        staffing: case_when([fn ($r) => $r->staff < 4, 'low'], [fn ($r) => $r->staff < 6, 'mid'], default: 'high'),
        volume: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visitors >= 250, 'busy', 'quiet'),
    )
    |> group_by('staffing', 'volume')
    |> summarise(mean_calls: mean('calls'), _groups: 'drop')
    |> mutate(mean_calls: fn ($r) => round($r->mean_calls, 2))
    |> pivot_wider(names_from: 'volume', values_from: 'mean_calls', names_sort: true)
    |> arrange(fn ($r) => array_search($r->staffing, ['low', 'mid', 'high']));

  staffing  busy quiet
  <chr>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 low      NA     1.9 
2 mid       1.79  1.64
3 high      1.8  NA

title: phplyr
text:
phplyr is a port of R’s dplyr and tidyr to PHP. It works on phibble tables. A pipeline is a method chain on PHP 8.3 and later, or uses the pipe operator on PHP 8.5, and reads like its R equivalent.
Each verb is a function that returns a closure taking one table. In a method chain, phplyr($t)->filter(...) runs filter() on the table, and get() returns the result. On PHP 8.5, the |> operator passes the table from one verb to the next. Verbs call the methods of phibble’s Table contract, so the same pipeline runs on the in-memory DataFrame and on other backends that implement the contract.
Results follow dplyr 1.2 and tidyr 1.3. The test suite runs the same pipelines in R and PHP and compares the output. The reference scripts are in tests/r/.

title: phplyr
text:
Install
phplyr needs PHP 8.3 or later. The pipe operator needs PHP 8.5.
composer require phpstats/phplyr
The optional phit extension speeds up the descriptive helpers and provides lm() and glm().

title: phplyr
text:
Where to go next

Getting started covers imports, loading data, and how verbs, row closures, and vector helpers fit together.
Coming from dplyr lists the syntax differences and what is not supported.
The reference pages document each group of functions with runnable examples.
The gallery has longer analyses on small example datasets.

title: phplyr
text:
The family

phibble provides the typed data frame, CSV and database sources, and the Table contract.
phplyr provides the dplyr and tidyr verbs.
phit is a native extension for statistical models and descriptive statistics.
phpolars is a native extension that binds Polars. phibble’s PolarsTable uses it to run the same verbs in Polars.

title: Porting an R script
text: This page takes a typical R analysis of the schools data and translates it to PHP with phplyr and phit. The analysis reads a CSV file, cleans and reshapes it, summarises it, and fits a linear, a logistic, and a random-intercept model. Both scripts ran when the documentation was built. The output under each script is what it printed.

title: Porting an R script
text:
What changed in translation

Loading. read.csv() becomes DataFrame::fromCsv(). phibble infers column types like readr.
Pipes. On PHP 8.5, R’s |> stays |>. Each verb returns a closure that the pipe applies. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the pipeline becomes a method chain: phplyr($t)->verb(...), ending with ->get().
Column references. Bare names become strings, or col('x') inside expressions. score - prior_score becomes col('score')->sub(col('prior_score')). A row closure, fn ($r) => $r->score - $r->prior_score, also works.
Conditions. case_when(x < 4 ~ "low", .default = "high") becomes case_when([col('x')->lt(4), 'low'], default: 'high').
Renaming in select. select(prior = prior_score) becomes select(['prior' => 'prior_score']).
Column sets. c(prior, final) becomes ['prior', 'final'].
Models. lm(), glm(), and lmer() take the same formulas. They return arrays with columns (R’s coefficient names), coefficients, standard errors, and fit statistics instead of model objects, so coef() and fixef() become array reads.
Printing. DataFrames print in tibble’s format. R rounds printed numbers to significant digits; phibble does the same.

Because the PHP pipeline uses col() expressions instead of closures, it also runs unchanged on a database table from Phibble\tbl(). See Databases and expressions.

title: Grouping
text:
group_by() sets the grouping columns. Selectors work, named arguments group by a computed column, and _add: true adds to the existing groups. _drop: false keeps groups for unused factor levels, so summarise() and count() return them with n() = 0, as dplyr does. ungroup() removes grouping, or only the named columns.
Groups are ordered like dplyr’s: sorted by key, factors by level order, and NA last. filter(), mutate(), summarise(), and the slice functions work within groups. _by: groups for a single call and returns an ungrouped table.

title: Grouping
text:
Group utilities







Function

The grouping column names


n_groups()
The number of groups


group_size()
Rows per group


group_indices()
Each row’s 1-based group number


group_keys()
A table of group keys


group_rows()
Each group’s 1-based row numbers


group_data()
The group keys with a .rows list-column


group_trim()
The table regrouped without unused factor levels


group_nest(_key:, _keep:)
One row per group, with a list-column of tables


nest_by(...cols)
group_nest() as a rowwise table


with_groups(groups, verb)
The verb’s result under other groups, with the original grouping restored


group_split(_keep:)
A list of tables, one per group


group_map(fn ($table, $key))
A list of the function’s results


group_modify(fn ($table, $key))
A grouped table built from the returned tables


group_walk(fn ($table, $key))
The table, after calling the function per group


group_cols()
A selector for the grouping columns


cur_group_id()
The current group’s number, in mutate(), summarise(), and reframe()


cur_group_rows()
The current group’s row numbers, in mutate() and reframe()


cur_group()
The current group’s key as an array of column => value

title: Grouping
text:
Row-wise operations
rowwise() makes each row its own group. Closures in summarise() and vector helpers then see one row at a time. Optional id columns stay as groups in the result of summarise(). c_across(cols) gives the current row’s values of the selected columns, for helpers such as sum(c_across(starts_with('x'))).

Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['id' => 'a', 'q1' => 3, 'q2' => 5, 'q3' => null],
    ['id' => 'b', 'q1' => 4, 'q2' => 1, 'q3' => 2],
]))
    ->rowwise('id')
    ->summarise(total: fn ($row) => Stats::sum(
        [...$row->column('q1'), ...$row->column('q2'), ...$row->column('q3')],
        naRm: true,
    ));


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['id' => 'a', 'q1' => 3, 'q2' => 5, 'q3' => null],
    ['id' => 'b', 'q1' => 4, 'q2' => 1, 'q3' => 2],
])
    |> rowwise('id')
    |> summarise(total: fn ($row) => Stats::sum(
        [...$row->column('q1'), ...$row->column('q2'), ...$row->column('q3')],
        naRm: true,
    ));



# A tibble: 2 × 2
# Groups:   id [2]
  id    total
  <chr> <int>
1 a         8
2 b         7

title: Single-table verbs
Single-table verbs
Single-table verbs
Single-table verbs
text:
Summaries
summarise() returns one row per group. Each named argument is a summary helper or a closure that receives the group’s table and returns one value. With several grouping columns, the result drops the last one, as in dplyr. _groups accepts 'drop_last', 'drop', 'keep', and 'rowwise'.

Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv'))
    ->summarise(
        students: n(),
        schools: n_distinct('school'),
        median_hours: median('study_hours'),
        q90_score: quantile('score', 0.9),
        iqr_score: iqr('score'),
        top_school: fn ($g) => (phplyr($g)->slice_max('score', n: 1)->pull('school'))[0],
    );


echo DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv')
    |> summarise(
        students: n(),
        schools: n_distinct('school'),
        median_hours: median('study_hours'),
        q90_score: quantile('score', 0.9),
        iqr_score: iqr('score'),
        top_school: fn ($g) => ($g |> slice_max('score', n: 1) |> pull('school'))[0],
    );



# A tibble: 1 × 6
  students schools median_hours q90_score iqr_score top_school
     <int>   <int>        <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>     
1      250      12         6.66      86.1      15.3 school-06
reframe() is summarise() for summaries that return several values. Results are recycled to a common length within each group, and the output is ungrouped.

Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv'))
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->school <= 'school-02')
    ->group_by('school')
    ->reframe(
        p: [0.25, 0.5, 0.75],
        score: fn ($g) => array_map(fn ($p) => Stats::quantile($g->column('score'), $p), [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]),
    );


echo DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv')
    |> filter(fn ($r) => $r->school <= 'school-02')
    |> group_by('school')
    |> reframe(
        p: [0.25, 0.5, 0.75],
        score: fn ($g) => array_map(fn ($p) => Stats::quantile($g->column('score'), $p), [0.25, 0.5, 0.75]),
    );

title: tidyr
text: The tidyr verbs use tidyr’s argument names. Arguments that start with a dot in tidyr start with an underscore here.

title: tidyr
tidyr
text:
Missing combinations and values
complete() adds missing combinations of the given columns and fills other columns with NA, or with values from fill:. A column name expands to its unique values (a factor to its levels), nesting() keeps only combinations that occur, and a named list supplies the values. It works within groups. expand() returns only the combinations, and crossing() and expand_grid() build a new table from lists.

Method chain (PHP 8.3+)Pipe (PHP 8.5)


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
]))
    ->complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
])
    |> complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);

1 north     1    10
2 north     2     0
3 north     3    12
4 south     1     0
5 south     2     7

fill() carries values down or up over NA within groups (_direction: 'down' | 'up' | 'downup' | 'updown'). drop_na() drops rows with NA in the given columns, and replace_na() replaces NA per column.

    ['quarter' => 'Q3', 'year' => null, 'sales' => 14],
]))
    ->fill('year')
    ->replace_na(['sales' => 0]);

title: tidyr
Two-table verbs
Two-table verbs
Two-table verbs
text:
join_by()
join_by() builds dplyr’s join specifications. A string is an equality on the same column name, ['a' => 'b'] maps names, and a comparison of two col() expressions compares x’s column (left) with y’s (right). Every condition must hold.
join_by('id', col('t')->ge(col('start')), col('t')->lt(col('end')))
join_by('id', between('t', 'start', 'end'))        // start and end are y's columns
join_by('id', closest(col('t')->ge(col('start'))))  // the latest start at or before t
join_by(within('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))         // x's interval inside y's
join_by(overlaps('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))
For inequality, rolling, and overlap joins, keep defaults to dplyr’s behavior: equality keys are merged and the columns in other conditions are kept from both tables. keep: false is an error for these joins. Database tables run them in SQL, except right and full rolling joins, which load the rows.
nest_join() keeps every row of x and adds a list-column (name:, default 'data') holding each row’s matching rows of y as a table.
